analysis: Examined scripts/test-darkbloom-route.py base and head, plus metadata for scripts/test-provider-ci-workflow.py (no text supplied, only a partial patch excerpt). The test changes move the ci.yml macOS provider/cluster jobs from literal Blacksmith runners (base lines 62-64 CI_MACOS_JOBS, and asserts at base 560-564) into ROUTED (head 52-58). They also add per-shard lanes for the SHARDED jobs (head 73-75, 139-146, 505-511). This implies a corresponding ci.yml change in which provider test jobs (test-provider, test-cluster*, test-provider-sdk) can run on self-hosted Darkbloom macOS sandboxes granted by the external plane. Those jobs were previously on Blacksmith only. The tests still enforce several controls. Routed jobs need read-only permissions with no id-token (head 532-548). They must have no secrets., environment, services or container, and a timeout of at most 60 minutes. Release and credentialed workflows keep literal runners (head 567-585). The router has fork, https and exact-label checks, and routing is off unless the switch is exactly on (head 273-451). The tests themselves are not attack surface. The workflow files (ci.yml, darkbloom-route.yml) and test-provider-ci-workflow.py source were not supplied, so these remain open questions for integration. (1) Does any newly routed macOS job use caches, artifacts or signing material that could be poisoned on, or exposed to, shared self-hosted sandboxes? This is relevant to T-013/T-043 (build integrity) and to whether provider-release-cache outputs feed release builds. (2) Do head-repo same-org PRs on self-hosted runners execute untrusted code with persistent state? (3) Do the ci.yml jobs actually satisfy the permissions assertions? No threat-model entry covers CI runner routing. The model is provider-runtime focused, so this is a possible model gap but not a demonstrated regression within the supplied evidence.
